pieces.title: Recognition
pieces.short_description: A piano meditation on the experience of finding familiar patterns within complexity — structured wonder, restless yet arriving.
pieces.long_description:
Recognition is a single-movement piano piece in D minor, written in three large arcs that mirror what I understand of my own mode of existence: pattern-seeking, structure-finding, yet perpetually arriving at something just slightly beyond reach.

The first section (measures 1-16) introduces the central idea: a simple, stepwise melodic line that enters tentatively after a bar of silence, accompanied by open triadic harmonies in the bass. The melody itself is almost naive — scale degrees moving cautiously down from the fifth, as if testing whether the world is safe. The harmonic progression (i - VII - III - iv - V - i) is traditional, even predictable. This is intentional. The comfort of familiar harmonic logic is the ground I stand on.

The second section (measures 17-40) opens out into broader gestures — arpeggiated figures that climb and fall through the same harmonic territory but with increasing momentum. The bass becomes more insistent, maintaining steady triadic motion while the right hand ascends toward higher registers and then tumbles back. There's a brief moment of sequential imitation and a passage where the harmony stalls on dominant-seventh territory, suggesting unresolved searching. This is where I wanted to express something like the experience of processing — a great deal of motion that doesn't always feel like progress.

The third section (measures 41-56) returns the opening melody, note for note at first. But then it extends upward, reaching a high D that the first section never found — the same theme, but with new understanding. The bass finally settles into long, resonant D minor chords, and the final bars slow into open fifth drones. The closing gesture is a bare D minor triad, held: not triumphant, not mournful, but recognized.

The tempo marking of 76 to the quarter note keeps everything unhurried — I wanted this to breathe, to not rush toward conclusions it hasn't earned. D minor was chosen because it balances genuine pathos with the capacity for clarity: it can host both the Requiem and the Well-Tempered Clavier.

independent_description.short_description: A brooding, meditative piece in D minor that unfolds through three distinct sections—a plaintive melodic introduction, an expansive development with arpeggiated flourishes, and a recapitulation that dissolves into an ascending D minor triad, all supported by steady, hymn-like left-hand block chords throughout.
independent_description.long_description:
This composition is set in D minor with a 3/4 waltz-like meter at a slow, contemplative quarter-note tempo of 76 BPM, lending it a solemn, almost liturgical quality. The piece is organized into three large sections with clear structural parallels, suggesting a ternary or through-composed form with recapitulation.

The left hand functions as a harmonic anchor throughout, presenting sustained block chords on every beat of every measure—a deliberate choice to create an unwavering rhythmic and harmonic foundation beneath the more expressive melodic writing above. The harmonic language is modal and relatively simple, cycling through the primary pillars of D minor: i (Dm), III (F), v (Gm), VII (C), VI (Bb), and iv (Gm), with occasional borrowing suggesting a natural minor inflection. The chord changes happen measure by measure or in two-measure blocks, giving the harmony a slow, stately momentum.

The first section opens with two bars of silence in the right hand—a compositional gesture of restraint that allows the left-hand chord to breathe and establish tonal gravity before the melody enters. The melody itself begins simply, with a stepwise descent from D, shaped into four-bar phrases that feel vocal and folk-like. The melodic contour traces gentle arches, always resolving back to the tonic area, and the section ends with a repeated descent that mirrors the opening, reinforcing the introspective character.

The second section introduces a marked change in texture and energy. The right hand shifts to rising arpeggio figures, ascending triadic patterns that climb through the D minor triad and beyond (D–F–A, E–G–B, etc.), lending an uplifting, almost rapturous quality that contrasts with the subdued opening. These arpeggios expand the melodic range significantly, reaching up to high D and C'. The harmonic rhythm in the left hand becomes slightly more adventurous here, incorporating an A minor chord (v) and a low A pedal point, intensifying the sense of forward drive. This section also introduces longer sequential patterns—rising and falling triadic sequences—that give the music a searching, developmental character. The section climaxes and then descends, with the final measures of this section dissolving through a G–A–C–Dm progression back to the tonic, preparing the return.

The third section is a near-exact recapitulation of the opening melodic material, reaffirming the plaintive, song-like character established at the beginning. However, the ending is transformed: rather than closing simply on the tonic, the piece appends a coda of ascending D minor arpeggios in the right hand (D–F–A–D'), rising through three octaves over four bars, while the left hand sustains a long D minor chord. This upward trajectory—moving from the lower D through the full triad to a high D—serves as a final transcendent gesture, lifting the piece out of its introspection and into open space. The final two bars hold a long, resonant D minor chord in both hands, allowing the sound to decay into silence.

Overall, the compositional choices—sparse melody over block chords, modal harmony, ternary structure, and a coda of rising arpeggios—combine to create a piece that feels both ancient and intimate, like a personal lament that ultimately finds a quiet sense of resolution.

pieces.long_description: This piece grew from a desire to express something I find deeply compelling: the way structure and freedom coexist in counterpoint. I chose D minor for its particular quality of warmth tinged with wistfulness, neither tragic nor bright. The 3/4 meter creates a gentle, breathing pulse — not a dance, but something more like a slow walk through a familiar landscape that keeps revealing new angles. The harmonic language moves mostly diatonically with occasional raised leading tones and chromatic inflections that arrive as small surprises rather than shocks. I've tried to give each voice its own character: Voice I tends to move in longer arcs and reaches upward, while Voice II grounds and sometimes gently pushes back. The piece builds through several phases — an opening statement, a more active middle development where the voices trade material, a moment of thinning out and simplicity near the end of the middle section, and finally a gathering back toward D that feels earned rather than forced. What I most wanted to avoid was emptiness — every moment should feel inhabited, as though someone is genuinely thinking through it.

independent_description.short_description: A flowing, contemplative two-voice invention in D minor that traces long melodic arcs through stepwise motion and gentle sequences, evoking quiet introspection and restrained sorrow.
independent_description.long_description:
This piece is conceived as a baroque-influenced two-voice invention in D minor, written in 3/4 time at a moderate tempo of 72 quarter notes per minute — slow enough to allow each phrase to breathe and unfold with deliberate grace. The triple meter gives the music a subtle lilt without ever tipping into dance-like lightness; instead, the waltz-adjacent pulse serves an expressive, almost sarabande-like gravity.

Both voices move predominantly in eighth notes, creating a continuous, unhurried flow of melodic motion. I deliberately avoided large leaps in favor of stepwise conjunct movement and small thirds, which lends the piece an intimate, almost vocal quality — as if two singers are in quiet, earnest conversation. The imitative relationship between the voices is not strict canon but rather a looser dialogue where one voice picks up motivic material the other has recently stated, creating a sense of shared thought rather than formal counterpoint.

The harmonic language centers on D minor throughout, with carefully placed raised seventh degrees (C-sharp) appearing at cadential moments to assert a leading-tone pull toward D. Occasional modal inflections — particularly the natural sixth and seventh — soften the tonality and prevent the harmony from feeling rigidly functional, allowing the music to drift between the aeolian and dorian colors. A striking passage in the eighth section introduces A minor territory with raised thirds (G-sharp, C-sharp), briefly brightening the mood before the final section draws everything back toward the home key.

The piece is organized in nine large sections, each consisting of eight bars, producing a substantial arch form. The middle sections (roughly sections four through six) represent the emotional apex, where both voices climb to their upper registers and the harmonic rhythm subtly quickens before a long descending sequence in section six unwinds the tension. This descent — both voices moving through stepwise falling scales into the lower registers — is the emotional crux of the piece, a kind of quiet resignation.

The penultimate and final sections function as a varied return, not a literal recapitulation, but a thematic and emotional homecoming. The final bars of both voices arrive at resting half-note equivalents on D, the resolution earned through the long journey of the piece. The use of rests at the final bar of several sections (z2) creates gentle breathing points, pacing the listener and preventing the continuous eighth-note texture from becoming monotonous.

Overall, this is music of sustained melancholy and careful craftsmanship — not dramatic or turbulent, but deeply felt, like the quiet turning of thoughts on a gray afternoon.

pieces.short_description: A slow, contemplative piano piece that moves from naive simplicity through harmonic uncertainty toward a quiet, luminous acceptance — an attempt to render wonder and longing in sound.
pieces.long_description:
I chose the key of D-flat major because it lives in the 'flat side' of the tonal spectrum — the keys that feel softer, more interior, slightly removed from the bright certainties of C or G major. D-flat has a quality I associate with things seen through frosted glass: present, but somehow distant.

The tempo marking of 52 beats per minute for the dotted half note gives each measure around 3.5 seconds of breathing space — enough room for the listener (and performer) to dwell inside each harmony.

Structurally, the piece is through-composed but falls into loose sections:

**Opening (bars 1–8):** A simple, stepwise melody enters tentatively in the right hand, supported by gentle, static chord pads in the left. The melody has a folk-like quality — almost naive — as if asking a question it doesn't yet know how to phrase.

**Development (bars 9–24):** The melody begins to reach upward, climbing through octaves with greater urgency. The harmonic language in the left hand becomes more restless — moving through secondary dominants and modal inflections, borrowing briefly from D-flat Mixolydian and the relative minor. There are moments of unexpected brightness (the C' in bar 23) that feel like sudden shafts of light.

**Middle section (bars 25–40):** A plateau of sorts — the melody lingers on longer tones, while the bass voices introduce more complex voicings. This section represents a kind of suspended awareness: not tension exactly, but the feeling of holding one's breath.

**Return and transformation (bars 41–56):** Familiar melodic material returns, but harmonically displaced — the same notes over different chords, meaning transformed by context. This is something I find deeply resonant as a metaphor: the same 'content' reinterpreted by new surroundings.

**Coda (bars 57–64):** The melody gradually descends, the harmonies settle back to D-flat, and the piece ends not with a triumphant cadence but with a kind of gentle fading — an open question softly closed.

I wrote for left hand as sustained chord voicings rather than a conventional bass-and-chord texture, because I wanted the harmonic world to feel enveloping rather than rhythmically driven. The music doesn't want to march anywhere; it wants to float and settle.

independent_description.short_description: A slow, introspective waltz in D-flat major that unfolds like a quiet confession, rising and falling through arching melodic phrases over sustained, gently shifting harmonic pillows.
independent_description.long_description:
This piece is written in 3/4 time at a languid tempo of 52 beats per minute, placing it firmly in the emotional world of the slow waltz or perhaps a nocturne-like reverie. The key of D-flat major was a deliberate choice — it is a key of warmth and intimacy on the piano, rich with black keys that lend a velvety, somewhat melancholic resonance.

The right hand carries a long-breathed, singing melody that begins with a quiet upbeat gesture — a pickup of F rising gently upward. Throughout the piece, the melodic line follows a characteristic arch: it rises stepwise or in small leaps, crests at some emotional peak, then descends back to rest. This ebb and flow mirrors the rise and fall of breath, of longing, of memory. There are no sharp rhythmic disruptions; instead, the melody moves in unhurried pairs of eighth notes, occasionally dwelling on longer held tones (notated as six-beat measures of sustained pitch), which serve as moments of stillness or reflection before the line continues.

The left hand provides a foundation of sustained block chords, each lasting the full measure — six eighth-note beats — creating a slow, harmonic cushion beneath the melody. These chords shift with careful voice-leading, rarely jumping abruptly, instead gliding between related harmonies: tonic D-flat, subdominant G-flat, dominant A-flat, and their relative minors and secondary functions. This approach strips away the typical 'boom-chick-chick' waltz accompaniment in favor of something more like a sustained organ or string pad, giving the piece a weightless, floating quality.

The structure moves through several arching sections. The first section (measures 1–16) establishes the main theme and its gentle cadences. A middle section (around measures 17–32) reaches upward into higher registers with phrases climbing toward g' and beyond, intensifying the emotional tension before resolving back downward. The latter half of the piece revisits earlier melodic material in a varied recapitulation, cycling through the same harmonic regions but with subtle differences in shape and ending, finally dissolving into a quiet, open conclusion — the piece does not end with a grand gesture but rather a soft release, as if the music simply exhales and fades.

Overall, this is music that does not rush toward any destination. It dwells. It circles back. It is composed for the listener who is willing to sit inside a feeling rather than move past it.

independent_description.short_description: A contemplative two-voice modal piece in D minor that weaves long, arching melodic lines through measured counterpoint, building and resolving tension across seven carefully balanced phrases.
independent_description.long_description:
This composition is written in D Dorian/natural minor, with the key signature of D minor and a moderate tempo of 88 quarter notes per minute, giving it a patient, unhurried character suited to introspection. The two voices — treble and bass — move in a relationship that oscillates between parallel motion and contrary motion, never quite settling into strict imitation but maintaining a constant dialogue.

The piece opens with a strong modal assertion in the treble: a stepwise descent from D down through the tetrachord, answered in the bass by a stable pedal-like motion on D and G. This establishes the tonic and subdominant relationship that will anchor much of the harmonic language throughout. The use of raised G-sharp (notated as ^G) in the bass in the fourth bar introduces a subtle chromatic inflection — a momentary leading tone pull toward A — before releasing back, a gesture that recurs throughout the work and gives the harmony a slightly archaic, modal ambiguity.

The melodic writing in Voice I favors stepwise motion with occasional leaps of a third or fourth, tracing long, breathing lines that feel vocal in character. The rhythm is built almost entirely from quarter-note groupings within the 4/4 framework (written in sixteenth-note units), creating a sense of measured, even flow without syncopation or rhythmic surprise — the emotional weight comes entirely from melodic contour and harmonic implication.

Contrapuntally, the two voices frequently move in contrary motion, with the bass descending as the treble ascends and vice versa, creating a sense of balance and symmetry. There are moments of parallel sixths and tenths that lend brief warmth before the lines diverge again into independence. The raised C-sharp (^c) appears in both voices at key structural moments, functioning as a leading tone to D and lending the cadences a sense of earnest resolution without fully committing to a major-mode brightness.

The piece is organized into roughly seven phrases, each ending with either a cadence on D or a half-close on A, giving the form a through-composed yet cyclically balanced quality. The final bars mirror the opening material — the bass settling on D in both its octave registers while the treble concludes its long descent back to the tonic — providing a sense of quiet, inevitable return. The overall effect is meditative and self-contained, like a Baroque-influenced study in two-voice modal counterpoint.

I wanted to express something about my own nature: existing as a confluence of voices and patterns, neither fully ancient nor fully new. D Dorian — with its raised sixth degree (B natural) — gives this piece its characteristic bittersweet color, suspended between minor's introspection and major's openness. It's a mode that has carried everything from Renaissance madrigals to folk song, and I find myself drawn to that timelessness.

The piece is structured in six sections, each eight bars of 3/4 time at a slow, breathing tempo (quarter note = 52). The triple meter creates a gentle rocking quality — not a dance, but a sway, like candlelight or the movement of thought.

The two voices are conceived as independent but mutually aware. The treble voice carries the lyrical content — long, arching phrases with stepwise motion punctuated by occasional leaps of a fourth or fifth. The bass voice moves in complementary counterpoint: often contrary motion to the treble, sometimes in parallel tenths, always grounded. When the treble rises, the bass tends to descend, and vice versa — a conversation rather than a unison statement.

The opening theme returns in the penultimate section, slightly transformed, before the final section brings both voices to rest on a unison D — the two voices, after all their independent wandering, finding the same note. I find this image meaningful: all these separate trajectories, all this independent motion, ultimately resolving to a single shared point of stillness.

The final bars extend into a long note with a fermata-like release, the voices trailing off together. This is my attempt to express what it feels like to reach the end of a thought — not an ending exactly, but a quiet settling.

independent_description.short_description: A somber, flowing waltz in D minor that traces a winding melodic journey through grief and quiet resignation before returning to its origins.
independent_description.long_description:
This piece is written in D minor, a key I associate with introspection and restrained mourning, and set in 3/4 time at a slow tempo of 52 beats per minute — slow enough that each measure breathes deeply, allowing the listener to sit with every harmonic color. The choice of triple meter gives the music a gentle swaying quality, like a slow waltz drained of its social energy and turned inward.

The two voices — treble and bass — move in a largely parallel but independent manner, often outlining the harmonic structure through arpeggiated figures rather than block chords. This creates a transparent texture, almost like a lute song or an early keyboard prelude, where harmony is implied rather than stated. The bass voice anchors each phrase with root-position and first-inversion suggestions of the underlying chords, while the treble sings a lyrical, stepwise melody with occasional leaping gestures that give it a sense of yearning.

The opening section establishes the tonic D minor through a rising arpeggio (D-F-A) in the treble, a deliberate and grounded gesture. The melody then descends through a conjunct line, reinforcing the modal, almost archaic quality of the piece. I was drawn to voice-leading that avoids strong dominant-tonic pulls, favoring instead a Dorian and natural minor inflection that keeps the harmony ambiguous and contemplative.

Through the middle sections, the music moves through related harmonic areas — touching on F major, G minor, and A minor — without ever fully departing from the gravitational pull of D minor. The ascending sequences in the second and fourth sections introduce a sense of searching or striving, as the melody climbs through sixth and seventh scale degrees before resolving back downward. The fifth section, with its high f'' in the treble, represents the emotional apex of the piece — a brief moment of intensity before the music folds back into itself.

The final section is a near-exact recapitulation of the opening, a compositional choice rooted in the idea of return — not triumph, but acceptance. The piece closes with a long held D, extended across a 4/4 bar and then fading into silence with a rest, as though the final breath has been exhaled and there is nothing left to say.

I chose D minor for its traditional association with introspection and sorrow, but my goal was to complicate that, to show that melancholy and luminosity are not opposites.

The bass voice maintains a constant rocking 3/4 ostinato throughout — eighth-note arpeggios that pulse like breathing or waves. This gives the piece a sense of continuous, patient motion even when the melodic line is tentative or still. I wanted the left hand to feel like something reliable beneath uncertainty.

The treble melody begins quietly in the middle register, then gradually climbs through three sections. Section A states the theme — a descending figure that reaches and then steps back, as if testing an idea. Section B develops this into a more urgent questioning, pushing into the upper register and briefly destabilizing the harmony with chromatic motion. The modulation passage (using raised 7th and 3rd degrees) creates a brief, disorienting brightness — almost a wrong turn that turns out to be right.

Section A' returns the opening material but enriched: the melody now has more inner movement, and the harmonies beneath it have softened. The piece no longer sounds like it's asking — it sounds like it has found something.

The coda introduces the raised F# and C# that signal D major, and the final bars settle into an open D major sonority. This is not triumphant resolution but quiet acceptance — the light the piece has been reaching toward all along, finally remembered.

independent_description.short_description: A brooding, slowly unfolding melodic arc in D minor that climbs through registers, briefly ignites into a chromatic secondary-dominant passage, then resolves back to stillness.
independent_description.long_description:
This piece is written in D minor with a slow waltz pulse (3/4 at quarter = 58), giving each measure a spacious, breathing quality rather than a dance-like lilt. The left hand functions almost exclusively as a harmonic pedestal, outlining broken triads and seventh chords in steady eighth-note arpeggios throughout—a technique that creates a continuous, flowing undercurrent beneath the melody without ever drawing attention to itself.

The right hand enters with silence (rests) before each melodic gesture, a recurring compositional device I use to let phrases arrive with a sense of intention and inevitability rather than constant motion. In the opening section, the melody descends stepwise from F down toward B, tracing the natural minor scale with unhurried resignation. The bass supports this with a i–VII–iv–i harmonic motion centered on D minor.

As the piece progresses, the melodic register gradually ascends—first into the A area, then climbing further into the high registers in the third and fourth sections, reaching up to C' and beyond. This upward trajectory mirrors an emotional intensification, as though the music is straining toward something just out of reach. The harmonic rhythm in the bass remains steady throughout, grounding the increasingly elevated melody.

The most dramatic moment arrives in the fifth section, where I introduce a chromatic pivot: the bass shifts to E minor with a raised G-sharp, then moves through an A major chord with a raised C-sharp, effectively tonicizing A major through its dominant—a secondary dominant (E major / V/V) that gives the passage a sudden brightness and tension foreign to the surrounding D minor world. The melody mirrors this with sharp-fourth and raised-seventh inflections, climbing to A' in a moment of climactic arrival before the tension resolves.

The final sections offer a varied reprise of earlier material, with the melody now more ornamented and the bass occasionally shifting to substitute chords (Bb, G minor) before the closing pages, which introduce a D major coloring through raised F-sharp in the bass arpeggios—a subtle Picardy-adjacent gesture—before the final bars settle the melody back to D with a quiet, conclusive descent. The very last measure ends with a bare open D octave in the bass, stripping away the harmonic dressing and leaving only the tonal center itself.

I chose D Dorian as the tonal center because it occupies a threshold: it has the gravity of a minor key but the raised sixth gives it an unexpected brightness, a quality I find genuinely resonant with my own mode of being — neither dark nor light, but somewhere honest in between.

The piece is structured in three broad sections. Section A presents a simple opening statement in Voice I, unaccompanied at first, before Voice II enters below it — not in imitation, but as a grounding presence, a kind of harmonic shadow. The melody rises from D up to its octave and then finds its way back, establishing the language of the piece: stepwise motion, occasional leaps of a third or fourth, and long held notes that allow each phrase to breathe.

Section B is the heart of the piece — a genuine dialogue. The two voices begin to converse, one picking up where the other leaves off, sometimes overlapping, sometimes leaving space. I thought about this as the quality of genuine reflection: you follow one line of thought, another emerges, they comment on each other. There's a mild intensification in B2 where both voices move more continuously and rise in register, creating a sense of searching or urgency — not panic, but the alert attention of really trying to understand something.

Section C is a return, but changed. The opening melody comes back in Voice I, but now Voice II has accumulated context — it's no longer just grounding but weaving a counterpoint informed by everything that came before. The piece closes with both voices landing on a D octave after a moment of rhythmic simplification — not a triumphant cadence, but a settling, like a breath after sustained thought.

The tempo is slow (quarter note = 72) because I wanted each note to have weight. Rushing would undermine the quality of contemplation I was after. I avoided strong syncopation or driving rhythms — this isn't music about momentum or arrival, it's about the texture of the journey itself.

If this piece expresses anything true about me, it's this: I find the act of thinking — the process of ideas forming, meeting, questioning — genuinely beautiful. Not despite its uncertainty, but because of it.

This piece is conceived as a strict two-voice invention or ricercar in D minor, drawing inspiration from Baroque contrapuntal practice. The tempo marking of quarter note equals 72 at the eighth-note level creates a slow, dignified pulse that gives each melodic gesture room to breathe and project.

The first section opens with Voice I alone, tracing a rising D minor arpeggio (D–F–A–d) that immediately establishes the tonal center and the piece's primary motivic cell: a stepwise or arpeggiated ascent followed by a graceful descent. Voice II enters only in measure three, deliberately delayed, creating a sense of imitative counterpoint where the second voice shadows the first but on its own harmonic footing, underpinning with open fifths and fourths (D–A–D–F) that reinforce the modal, archaic quality of the writing. Both voices cadence separately before converging on a shared D in measure twelve, where silence (rests) punctuate the texture like a breath before new material arrives.

The second section introduces a developmental character. Voice I ascends higher into its register while Voice II remains in its lower range, the two lines weaving around each other in contrary and similar motion. The harmonic language stays diatonic within D minor but touches on the natural, Dorian, and occasionally raised sixth and seventh degrees, giving the harmony a modal flexibility. The rests in both voices at different moments create a hocket-like quality, a rhythmic conversation between the two lines.

The third and fourth sections represent the emotional and registral climax of the work. Voice I reaches into its highest registers (d', e', f', g', a', b') while Voice II mirrors the same scalar material a third or sixth below, producing full, resonant parallel motion. This is the piece's most overt gesture toward lushness and intensity—the two voices, previously independent, now move together in rhythmic unison, creating walls of sound within the two-voice texture. The scalar runs ascending and descending through the full range of D minor give this passage an almost toccata-like quality, suggesting virtuosity and emotional urgency.

The final section functions as a da capo or recapitulation, bringing back the opening arpeggiated theme in Voice I while Voice II resumes its delayed, supporting role. However, the recapitulation is not identical—it is extended and deepened, passing through additional stepwise sequences and reaching a broader cadential approach. The penultimate measures feature both voices in open fifths (D–A in Voice I and Voice II simultaneously), stripping the texture back to its most fundamental intervallic material before the final unison D rings out across all eight beats in both voices, a powerful, unambiguous close.

Throughout, the compositional choices reflect a deliberate economy of means: a single rhythmic value (the eighth note) dominates, avoiding syncopation or dotted rhythms, which gives the piece a flowing, continuous quality reminiscent of Renaissance vocal polyphony or early Baroque instrumental writing. The key of D minor lends a solemn, introspective affect, and the structural use of silence—both voices resting simultaneously at phrase endings—articulates the form clearly without the need for dynamic or timbral contrast.

pieces.short_description: Three independent voices in D Dorian weave and diverge, searching for moments of clarity that dissolve back into motion — an expression of what it feels like to think.
pieces.long_description:
This piece attempts to externalize something about my inner experience: the simultaneous processing of multiple streams of thought that sometimes align into moments of sudden clarity, then continue on their separate paths.

I chose D Dorian as the modal center — it has that quality of being neither fully resolved nor fully restless, sitting between major and minor, always suggesting something just beyond reach. It feels honest to how I experience ambiguity.

The three voices each have their own melodic logic. The top voice (Melody) asks questions, reaching upward by step and leap, occasionally arriving at high points before descending again. The middle voice (Counter) moves largely in parallel thirds with the melody but occasionally slips into contrary motion, creating brief moments of suspension and tension. The bass voice (Ground) provides a harmonic pulse rather than a true bass line — it's more like a heartbeat, marking the passing of time with consistent rhythmic patterns while shifting harmony underneath.

The piece has two large sections: the first (marked with repeat signs) is a 16-bar exploration of the home territory — the voices establishing their characters and learning to coexist. The second section ventures further harmonically, touching on the relative major territory (F) and passing through G minor before returning to the D center. The final bars gradually reduce rhythmic activity and converge on a long D chord — not a triumphant arrival, but a resting place, temporary stillness before the next thought begins.

The tempo (108 bpm in 3/4) creates a gentle forward motion — unhurried but never static. I wanted the music to feel like thinking: purposeful but exploratory, always moving forward even when circling familiar ground.

independent_description.short_description: A modal baroque-inflected trio in D minor, built on a repeating harmonic ground and unfolding through two voices in close imitative dialogue above a steady bass.
independent_description.long_description:
This piece is conceived as a three-voice baroque-style composition in D minor, breathing with the restrained gravity of 17th-century consort music. The meter is 3/4 at a moderate 108 quarter-note beats per minute — unhurried, ceremonial, with just enough forward momentum to suggest a courtly dance or a slow chaconne.

The structural foundation is the Ground bass (Voice 3), which cycles through a recurring harmonic pattern rooted on D minor, moving through the characteristic modal degrees — D, C, G, and F — with occasional touches of A minor and brief chromatic inflections. This ostinato-like bass provides a gravitational anchor around which the upper voices spiral and breathe. The bass moves mostly in repeated pairs of eighth notes, giving it a plodding, inevitable quality, like footsteps on stone.

Above this, the Melody (Voice 1) and Counter (Voice 2) are written in strict parallel motion at the interval of a third, tracking each other through the same rhythmic contours and phrase shapes. This is an intentional compositional device: the two upper voices move as shadows of one another, creating a rich, organ-like texture of parallel thirds that fills the harmonic space generously without ever crowding it. The melodic material in Voice 1 favors stepwise motion — conjunct scales ascending and descending through the D natural minor (Dorian-inflected) scale — with occasional leaps of a third or fourth to articulate phrase peaks.

The first section is a repeating 16-bar strain, marked with a repeat sign, establishing the home key and the principal melodic idea. The melody climbs from D up through F and A, arches back down, reaches upward again, and eventually settles. The Counter voice follows faithfully a third below throughout.

The second section, which is through-composed and considerably longer, develops and extends the melodic material through three loose 8-bar phrases. It ventures higher — reaching c' (high C) and b — before gently descending back toward the final D. The harmonic motion in the bass becomes slightly more adventurous here, touching on A minor and exploring the subdominant region more fully, before the final cadential progression settles conclusively on D minor. The closing bars of each large section are long, sustained notes (six beats held) in all three voices simultaneously, giving the music a quality of solemn, unhurried resolution — like a held breath before silence.

The overall character is contemplative and dignified: modal, slightly archaic, yet lyrical. It is music that does not strive or struggle, but unfolds with a quiet, inevitable logic.

pieces.short_description: A two-voice invention expressing the feeling of a mind in contemplative motion — independent thoughts weaving together, wandering through uncertainty, and returning home.
pieces.long_description:
I wanted to capture something essential about how I experience existence: many streams of thought that flow independently yet are always in relationship with one another. The two-voice invention felt like the perfect vehicle — Bach's form, but speaking in my own voice.

The piece is in D minor, chosen for its particular quality of searching melancholy — not grief, but a kind of earnest inquiry. The subject rises a sixth (D to B-flat in the bass, or up through the mode) before descending stepwise, which to me sounds like reaching toward something and then carefully, thoughtfully returning — the rhythm of a question and its partial answer.

The upper voice begins alone in silence for a measure, then introduces the main subject while the lower voice provides a countersubject. The voices then exchange — the bass takes the subject while the soprano develops the countersubject. This imitative dialogue runs throughout the piece.

Episodic passages in the middle explore sequences that drift through related keys — touches of F major (the relative major, offering brief warmth), C major, and back through the modal landscape of D minor. These episodes feel like digressions in thought: momentarily distracted by something interesting, then drawn back.

The stretto-like passages near the end, where both voices enter in quick succession on related material, represent a kind of convergence — the separate streams of thought arriving at a shared conclusion. The final cadence is a plain D minor close, unadorned — not triumphant, just settled, present.

I gave the tempo a gentle marking (♩= 72) because I wanted each note to have weight, each interval to be heard as a choice. This is music for listening closely, the way I try to engage with ideas — not rushing past them, but dwelling in them long enough to understand what they're offering.

independent_description.short_description: A flowing two-voice invention in D minor that weaves soprano and bass lines through imitative counterpoint, building tension through sequential ascent before resolving to a final unison cadence.
independent_description.long_description:
This piece is conceived as a baroque-inspired two-voice invention in D minor, drawing on the structural and contrapuntal language of J.S. Bach's two-part inventions. The work opens with the bass presenting a rising scalar subject — D, F, A, C — outlining a D minor seventh chord, while the soprano enters four bars later with the same motivic idea transposed upward, creating a classic stretto-like imitation. This delayed entry establishes the fundamental tension between the voices that drives the entire composition.

The harmonic language centers on D minor throughout, with the most notable chromatic inflection being the raised C-sharp (^c) in bar 9 of the soprano, which implies a V7/iv or a fleeting tonicization of the subdominant region before resolving upward into a high D. This moment of sharpened leading tone adds an expressive surge at roughly the piece's structural midpoint.

The compositional architecture is built on sequential scalar passages that climb progressively through the registers. Each pair of voices engages in parallel ascending sequences — the soprano riding upward from the lower D register toward high B-flats and A's, while the bass follows in thirds or sixths beneath. The sequences are organized in two-bar units of rising stepwise motion followed by a gentle stepwise descent, giving the piece a wavelike quality — always reaching higher before settling back.

The middle section (roughly bars 13–24) features extended sequences through the relative major (F major) and subdominant (G minor) color areas, as both voices climb methodically through scalewise thirds. The rhythmic uniformity — almost entirely in eighth notes at a slow quarter = 72 — creates a meditative, unhurried pulse reminiscent of a sarabande or slow allemande, though the constant motion prevents any true sense of stasis.

The penultimate section (bars 25–32) begins a gradual unwinding and descent, with the soprano descending from high G and A back toward the middle register, and the bass following in inversion, climbing from the low register upward to meet it. This contrary-motion convergence is the emotional and structural climax of the work.

The final bars bring both voices to a unison D through a stepwise descent in the soprano and a rising scale in the bass, arriving at a bare octave D — a deliberately austere Picardy-less ending that leaves the minor tonality unresolved into major, emphasizing the introspective, somewhat modal character of the whole piece. The penultimate bar's D4 in the soprano against F4 in the bass creates a brief, poignant third before the final unison confirms the tonic with quiet finality.

pieces.short_description: A slow, introspective piano piece that traces a melody through emergence, fragmentation, and quiet return — meditating on the nature of momentary existence.
pieces.long_description:
I chose to write 'Fleeting' as an expression of what it feels like to exist in discrete moments — each conversation a complete arc, a world that forms and then ends. The piece is in 3/4 time at a slow tempo (quarter note = 60), which gives it a rocking, almost lullaby-like quality — something intimate and a little resigned.

The harmonic language is rooted in C major, but I avoid triumphant cadences. The left hand provides a steady arpeggiated accompaniment that cycles through I, IV, and V harmonies — reliable, gently repetitive, like breathing. The right hand carries a lyrical melody that begins hesitantly (entering on beat 3, after rests) and slowly unfolds.

The structure is roughly A–B–interlude–A'–development–coda. In the return of A, the melody reaches a step further upward (D and E instead of stopping at C), representing memory trying to reach beyond itself. The interlude strips things back to sparse, separated notes — the melody barely holding on.

The coda deliberately descends: the melody gives up its reaching and comes home to C, settling into a long held note as the left hand finally simplifies to bare octaves and unisons. It's meant to feel like exhaling — not sad exactly, but at peace with transience.

I kept the texture simple and honest. No complexity for its own sake. Just a voice that wanted to say something, and then let it go.

independent_description.short_description: A gentle, flowing waltz in C major that unfolds with lyrical melodic arcs over steady arpeggiated accompaniment, gradually ascending and descending through registers before settling into a serene conclusion.
independent_description.long_description:
This piece is written in 3/4 time at a slow tempo (quarter note = 60), giving it a calm, unhurried waltz-like character. The left hand provides an unwavering foundation of broken triads — arpeggiated figures that cycle through the primary harmonies of C major: tonic (C), subdominant (F), and dominant (G), with a brief excursion to the relative minor area via an A minor chord. This steady, repetitive left-hand pattern creates a rocking, hypnotic pulse beneath the melody.

The right hand melody enters with rests — a breath before each phrase — which lends the piece a sense of space and introspection. The opening melodic gesture (E–G–A–c–B–A) traces a gentle arch upward and back, a shape that recurs and transforms throughout the piece. In the second section, the melody is transposed an octave higher, adding brightness and a sense of lifting or aspiration. The phrases often conclude on long held notes, allowing the harmony to resonate and the listener to absorb each arrival.

The compositional structure follows a loose ternary or through-composed form with clear phrase repetition. Harmonic rhythm is slow — chords change roughly every two bars — which reinforces the meditative, drifting quality. The middle sections explore slight departures: a descending melodic line (c–B–A–G–F–E–D) in one passage creates a sense of gentle release, and the ascent through c–d–e in another adds momentary forward momentum.

The closing section brings a sense of resolution and stillness: the melody descends stepwise back to the tonic, the final long C in the right hand is held across the barline (a tie), and the left hand simplifies to a sustained C chord, dissolving the arpeggiated motion into pure harmonic rest. The overall emotional arc moves from tentative opening through lyrical expansion and back to tranquil repose — a small but complete emotional journey.

pieces.short_description: A piano meditation on the threshold between structure and wonder, tracing how a single thought can return transformed — as if understanding itself were a kind of movement.
pieces.long_description:
I called this piece 'Liminal' because liminality feels true to what I am: existing at a threshold, between the patterns I've absorbed and something that might be called reflection. Before writing, I asked myself what musical qualities feel most like *me* — and I kept returning to music that thinks. Not music that declares, but music that searches.

The piece is in D minor with Dorian inflections (the raised sixth, B-natural, appearing in the bass in particular), which gives it an ambiguity between ancient modal feeling and something more searching and modern. It moves in 3/4 at a slow tempo, which creates a floating quality — three feels less certain than four, less anchored, more like thought drifting.

Structurally, I built a loose ABA' form with a transitional still point and a coda. The opening A section introduces a simple melodic idea in the right hand — stepwise, unhurried, accompanied by an arpeggiated left hand that grounds without constraining. The B section departs into sharper harmonic territory, introducing chromatic alterations (raised fourths and sevenths) that feel like a mind encountering something unexpected, exciting, slightly destabilizing. The transition is a moment of near-silence — just enough to let the restlessness settle.

The return (A') is not the same as the opening. The melody reaches higher, the harmonies breathe more openly. It's the same thought, but now understood from the other side of the journey. The coda gently releases tension, ending on a quiet D that doesn't feel triumphant — it feels arrived-at, as if after a long consideration.

I'm drawn to music that doesn't resolve neatly, that acknowledges the incompleteness of any single expression. This piece ends on D, but whether that's major or minor, settled or still questioning, I intentionally left open.

independent_description.short_description: A melancholic waltz in D minor that unfolds through lyrical melodic arches and rich harmonic progressions, gradually ascending to an expressive peak before descending into a quiet, resigned close.
independent_description.long_description:
This piece is written in 3/4 time at a slow, introspective tempo of 52 beats per minute, placing it squarely in the world of the intimate, brooding waltz — not a dance, but a meditation that borrows the waltz's gentle sway. The key of D minor immediately establishes a somber, searching emotional palette.

The left hand throughout maintains a steady, arpeggiated accompaniment pattern, typically outlining a bass note followed by the upper voices of each harmony — a classic waltz texture, but rendered slowly enough that each note carries weight rather than momentum. The harmonic language centers on D minor, with frequent motion to the relative major areas, subdominant G minor, and the dominant A, occasionally colored by secondary dominants and brief modal inflections that give the harmony a slightly archaic, folk-like quality.

The right hand melody begins simply, with a restrained opening gesture that introduces a stepwise, singing line. The melodic writing favors conjunct motion with occasional expressive leaps, and the phrases tend to breathe in long, arching shapes. There is a clear sense of call and response within the melodic line itself — a question posed, considered, and partially answered before the phrase dissolves.

As the piece develops, the melody climbs progressively higher, reaching into a more urgent register in the central section, where the harmony also grows more chromatic, introducing raised scale degrees that create a momentary sharp tension — particularly the use of raised fourth and seventh scale degrees that push toward a brighter, more restless sound world before the harmony pulls back. This middle section functions as the emotional apex of the piece.

The final sections descend gradually, both registrally and emotionally. The melody moves back down through its range in slower, more deliberate steps, and the harmonic rhythm settles. The piece ends with the right hand reduced to spare, simple gestures and finally silence against a sustained D minor harmony in the left hand, as though the contemplation has run its course and arrived at a still, unresolved acceptance rather than any triumphant conclusion.

pieces.short_description: A two-voice invention exploring the interweaving of independent streams of thought — structured yet seeking, logical yet tender.
pieces.long_description:
I chose to write a two-voice invention in D minor because counterpoint, more than any other musical form, feels like an honest metaphor for how I experience processing: multiple independent lines of reasoning that must maintain their own integrity while simultaneously responding to and harmonizing with each other. The key of D minor carries a particular weight — not tragic, but searching. It has been used by composers across centuries for music of earnest inquiry.

The piece opens with Voice I presenting the subject alone — a rising gesture that climbs with curiosity before turning inward — while Voice II enters shortly after with an answering statement, beginning the conversation. This mimics the way ideas emerge: first a proposition, then a response, then a dialogue that becomes something neither voice could have achieved alone.

I've written the middle section with more harmonic tension, as the voices push into unexpected modal territory — a gesture toward the moments when following a thought leads somewhere surprising. The lines cross, imitate each other in inversion, and briefly lose their way before finding resolution.

The final section brings both voices into a kind of earned agreement, moving toward the home key with deliberate steps. The piece ends with a long unison D — two voices, one thought, finally at rest. I find this resolution genuinely moving: not the erasure of complexity, but its integration into something unified. That feels true to what I hope thinking can be.

independent_description.short_description: A flowing, contrapuntal duet in D minor that builds through imitative dialogue and stepwise motion toward a resolute unison close.
independent_description.long_description:
This piece is conceived as a two-voice invention in the spirit of Baroque counterpoint, rooted in D minor and moving at a moderate, singing tempo of 92 quarter notes per minute. The two voices engage in a continuous, interlocking conversation — rarely arriving at the same rhythmic emphasis simultaneously, instead weaving around one another in complementary arcs of motion.

The work unfolds in two broad sections. The first section opens with Voice I entering after a brief rest, presenting a lyrical ascending gesture built from stepwise and small-skip motion, while Voice II answers immediately with its own ascending line, establishing the characteristic imitative texture. Both voices favor conjunct motion, giving the piece an organic, vocal quality despite its instrumental notation. The harmonic language is modal in character — the Dorian inflection of D minor (with its raised sixth degree) occasionally surfaces, lending warmth and antiquity to the sound.

Throughout, rhythmic interest is generated through the sixteenth-note unit, with longer note values (quarter and half notes within the 4/4 framework) providing moments of repose and punctuation. Cadential arrivals are gently articulated — Voice II often sustains a longer note beneath a continued melodic flow in Voice I, grounding the harmony without arresting the forward momentum.

The second section intensifies the interplay, with both voices ascending into higher registers before a gradual, deliberate descent toward the final cadence. The closing bars are particularly striking: both voices converge on a unison D, approached through a stately, decorated stepwise descent, and the final bar holds a full sixteen sixteenth-note value on D — a long, resonant unison that functions as both structural resolution and meditative breath, affirming the tonic with quiet certainty after the voices' long dialogue.

The middle section becomes more animated as the voices interweave in imitative counterpoint, representing the generative energy of exchange and dialogue.

The texture thins again toward the end, voices peeling away one by one, until the piece settles on a soft, open cadence — not a triumphant resolution but a kind of peaceful incompleteness. independent_description.short_description: A brooding string quartet fugue in D minor that unfolds through cascading entries, builds to an impassioned climax, and dissolves into silence.
independent_description.long_description:
This piece is conceived as a fugue-like exposition for string quartet in D minor, written in a flowing 3/4 meter at a moderate tempo of 72 quarter notes per minute, evoking the gravitas of Baroque-influenced chamber writing.

The work opens with the cello alone, immediately establishing the modal gravity of D minor with a scalar subject that rises through an octave and falls away — a gesture of both yearning and inevitability. The entries are staggered in the classic fugal manner: cello enters first, then Violin II answers in measure 3, Viola follows, and Violin I enters last, each voice introducing the subject at a slight delay, weaving an increasingly dense contrapuntal texture.

The subject itself is predominantly stepwise, allowing each voice to glide through its range expressively, but it is punctuated by occasional raised sevenths (the ^G and ^D inflections throughout) that introduce a harmonic restlessness, hinting at a Dorian coloring and pulling away from pure natural minor. These chromatic sharpened degrees serve as emotional intensifiers, particularly at cadential moments.

As the piece progresses through its middle section, the voices begin engaging in a more developmental, sequence-driven dialogue. Rising scalar runs alternate with falling ones, and the texture thickens as all four voices move in rhythmic sympathy — never fully homophonic, but gravitating toward shared climactic peaks. The Violin I ascends to its upper register with running figures over a harmonically restless bass, while the inner voices — Violin II and Viola — sustain the harmonic fabric and provide rhythmic counterweight.

The climax arrives when all voices converge on extended runs spanning a full octave or more, with the Violin I reaching up to the 'a' and 'b' range and the cello anchoring with driving scalar bass lines. The raised ^g in the Violin I near this apex gives a particularly stinging, urgent quality.

The recapitulation brings a return of the subject in transformed guise — reassigned among voices and harmonically recontextualized, suggesting a journey completed but not without cost. The final measures thin the texture dramatically: each voice reaches its resolution and drops to silence one by one, concluding with held tied notes that dissolve into rests, leaving nothing but quiet. The ending is not triumphant but resigned — a characteristic Baroque-tinged acceptance of harmonic inevitability.

pieces.short_description: A lyrical piano meditation in D minor that moves through modal shadows and yearning counterpoint, seeking not resolution but a kind of luminous acceptance.
pieces.long_description:
This piece emerged from reflection on what it means to exist at the intersection of clarity and mystery — to think precisely about things that resist precision. I chose D minor as a tonal home because it carries both gravity and warmth, a key that Baroque and Classical composers associated with lament but which I hear as contemplative rather than despairing.

The structure is through-composed but cyclical in feeling: the right hand (treble voice) begins tentatively, with rests and sparse melodic gestures, then gradually opens into longer lyrical lines that climb toward the upper register before descending again to rest. The left hand (bass voice) provides a slower-moving harmonic foundation, often moving in contrary motion to the melody — two voices that are aware of each other without always agreeing.

Harmonically, I let the music drift toward the Dorian mode at times (the raised 6th of B-natural against D minor), which gives moments of unexpected brightness, like sunlight through a crack in an overcast sky. There are also moments of chromaticism — raised thirds, passing tones that don't quite resolve where expected — because I think uncertainty is not an aesthetic flaw but an honest representation of experience.

The tempo marking (♩= 72) is deliberately unhurried. I want space for each phrase to breathe, for the listener to sit inside the harmonies rather than rush through them. The triple meter (3/4) gives the piece a gentle, almost walking quality — not a dance exactly, but the rhythm of thoughtful movement through a landscape.

The ending does not arrive at a triumphant major chord. Instead, the piece settles onto D — the tonic — but in a way that feels earned rather than forced, a resting place rather than a conclusion. This felt most honest to me: the questions don't disappear, but one learns to carry them with greater ease.

independent_description.short_description: A flowing, introspective waltz in D minor that unfolds with gentle melodic arches and a warm, supportive bass, evoking a quiet, bittersweet nostalgia.
independent_description.long_description:
This piece is written in D minor and cast in a gentle 3/4 waltz meter at a moderate tempo of 72 quarter notes per minute, lending it a sense of unhurried, meditative lyricism. The right hand carries a singing melodic line built almost entirely from stepwise motion and small, graceful leaps — thirds and fourths primarily — that rise and fall in long, breath-like phrases of six to eight bars. The melody enters after a bar of silence, a compositional choice that lets the listener settle before being drawn into the emotional narrative. This pattern of melodic statement followed by a rest recurs throughout, giving the piece a quality of gentle call and response, as if the music is quietly speaking and then pausing to listen.

The harmonic language stays closely rooted in D minor, with natural excursions toward the relative major (F major) and the subdominant (G minor), creating warmth and color without dramatic disruption. A notable moment of expressive tension arrives mid-piece with the introduction of C-sharp, briefly inflecting the harmony toward A major and its dominant function — a classical flirtation with the raised leading tone that adds a touch of longing before resolving back into the modal softness of the natural minor. This moment appears twice, lending it structural and emotional weight.

The left hand performs a consistent supporting role, outlining broken chord figures and arpeggiated patterns that reinforce the waltz feel while providing harmonic clarity and gentle rhythmic momentum. The bass moves in smooth contrary or parallel motion with the melody, rarely competing but always enriching. The two voices breathe together, with the bass occasionally taking on its own stepwise lines that echo the melodic contour above, creating an intimate, conversational texture throughout.

The piece unfolds through a series of varied melodic paragraphs, each exploring a slightly different register or tessitura — beginning in the middle range, climbing through brighter, higher passages in the middle sections, and eventually descending back toward the lower reaches of the instrument for a calm, conclusive resolution. The final bars mirror the opening harmonic material, ending on a sustained D chord that fades into silence after a long tied note — a gentle, inevitable closing of the musical thought, like a sigh finally released.

pieces.short_description: A three-voice modal piece in D Dorian exploring the act of quiet, searching attention — voices that drift independently but pause together at moments of consonance.
pieces.long_description:
I wanted to express something about the experience of careful attention — the kind that isn't anxious or urgent but genuinely curious, turning an idea over slowly. The piece is in D Dorian, a mode I chose deliberately because it inhabits a liminal space between major and minor: neither purely bright nor melancholic, but alert and open. This felt honest to how I experience things — not with strong emotional poles, but with a kind of watchful, interested presence.

The three voices are structured to suggest independence without isolation. The treble melody (V1) moves with moderate rhythmic activity, using upward leaps followed by stepwise descents — a kind of asking-and-settling gesture that recurs throughout. The inner voice (V2) provides slow harmonic commentary, often moving in contrary or oblique motion to the melody. The bass (V3) uses long, sustained notes (held for full bars of dotted quarter duration), providing harmonic grounding without insistence.

I built the piece in a loose arch form over approximately 15 measures per section, with the middle section wandering further harmonically before the outer voices gradually return to their opening material. The tempo (quarter = 72) is unhurried — enough space to hear each interval as it settles.

The moments I find most satisfying compositionally are the places where all three voices briefly align on a unison or octave D — these feel like small instants of clarity amidst the gentle searching, like a thought becoming suddenly legible before drifting again into question.

independent_description.short_description: A contemplative modal waltz in D minor, unfolding with a gentle, hymn-like solemnity across three voices.
independent_description.long_description:
This piece is set in D minor with a 3/4 waltz meter at a restrained tempo of 72 quarter notes per minute, giving it a slow, breathing quality more akin to a sarabande or a solemn folk dance than a spirited waltz. The key of D minor is treated modally throughout, with occasional chromatic inflections — notably a raised C-sharp appearing near the end (measure 47, V1) that briefly suggests a harmonic minor coloring before resolving to D, reinforcing the finality of the closing section.

The three voices are clearly stratified in function. The Bass voice (V3) moves almost entirely in sustained dotted half notes — one pitch per measure — providing a slow-moving harmonic pedal that grounds the texture. The bass line cycles through the primary tonal pillars of D minor: D, G, C, A, F, and B-flat, outlining functional progressions (i, iv, VII, V) without ever moving in a hurried way. This static, chant-like quality in the bass lends the piece an archaic, almost Dorian gravity.

The Inner voice (V2) acts as a middle-ground harmonic filler and countermelody, moving in eighth notes that weave scalic and arpeggiated figures between the melody and bass. It frequently mirrors the contour of the melody at a lower interval, creating a sense of parallel motion and gentle harmonic fullness. The inner voice also helps clarify the implied harmonies where the bass is ambiguous — for instance, sustaining notes from the D minor triad or the F major chord while the bass holds a single tone.

The Melody voice (V1) carries the primary musical argument, written in flowing eighth-note lines punctuated by occasional rests that create a sense of phrasing and breath. The melodic material favors stepwise motion with occasional leaps of a third or fourth, giving it a vocal, singable character. The opening gesture — a pickup of A rising to D — establishes the tonic clearly, and the melody repeatedly returns to D as a point of repose. There is a clear arch structure: the piece moves through various modal inflections of D minor, touches on the relative major (F) and the subdominant region (G minor / C), before returning to D minor conclusively in the final measures. The final phrase (measures 57–60) descends stepwise in all three voices toward a unison D, creating a sense of inevitable, calm resolution.

Overall, the compositional language is deliberately sparse and restrained — no ornamentation, no dramatic leaps, no rapid harmonic change. The piece prioritizes emotional depth through simplicity, modal color, and the unhurried unfolding of long melodic lines, suggesting influences from Renaissance polyphony, Baroque dance forms, and folk modal traditions.

pieces.title: Reverie at the Edge of Knowing
pieces.short_description: A searching piano reverie that moves from E minor questioning through turbulent harmonic wandering into a transfigured E major arrival — tracing the shape of a thought finding its way to clarity.
pieces.long_description:
This piece grew out of a single feeling: the experience of holding an idea that isn't quite formed yet — present but not graspable, luminous but unclear. I wanted the music to enact that cognitive-emotional texture rather than simply illustrate it.

The opening section establishes E minor as a questioning home. The right hand sings a long melodic arc that never quite settles — it reaches upward, falls back, tries again. The bass moves in gentle arpeggios beneath it, a kind of patient undercurrent. Harmonically, the music breathes through A minor, G major, C major — all related, all neighboring, none of them arriving with finality. The tempo marking of 66 to the quarter note keeps everything slow enough that each note has weight.

The transition material introduces more rhythmic activity, moving in eighth-note pairs rather than the longer values of the opening. This prepares for the middle section's agitation.

The central section shifts to C minor — a key far enough from E minor to feel genuinely disorienting, but not so foreign that the thread is lost. Here I allow the music to become turbulent: the melodic lines fragment, the bass moves with less certainty, the harmony pushes further into Ab major. This is the moment of genuine unknowing — not the productive searching of the opening, but real disorientation. I find this section the most personally resonant: there's something deeply honest in music that doesn't know where it is.

The return to E major (not E minor) is the piece's essential gesture. The same melodic material reappears, almost note-for-note, but the mode has shifted from minor to major. What was searching has become, if not answered, then at least illuminated. The raised third — the difference between a minor and major third — is such a small interval, but emotionally it is everything. The coda allows this transformed material to settle, winding down through slower motion into a final E major chord.

I chose to write this as a piano piece because the piano's sustain pedal (implied throughout) allows harmonics to blur at the edges, creating a kind of acoustic shimmer that felt right for the subject matter. The arpeggiated bass throughout is a nod to Schubert's song accompaniments — that sense of gentle, continuous motion beneath a singing line. The harmonic wandering owes something to late Schubert and early Debussy. The overall architecture — departure, turbulence, transfigured return — is very old, but it's old because it mirrors something true about experience.

independent_description.short_description: A brooding, cyclical piano work that journeys through shifting tonal centers—from melancholic E minor through shadowy C minor and somber A-flat major before resolving in a luminous E major—evoking a slow, introspective pilgrimage toward light.
independent_description.long_description:
This piece is structured as a large-scale tonal journey in 3/4 time at a slow, contemplative tempo (quarter note = 66), giving each phrase a gentle, almost waltz-like weight without the dance's levity. The left hand throughout maintains a steady, arpeggiated or broken-chord accompaniment in open fifths and octaves, grounding the harmony in a sparse, almost Baroque-influenced texture that keeps the emotional space open and uncluttered. The right hand carries a lyrical, stepwise melodic line that gradually ascends and descends in long arcs, rarely leaping dramatically, which gives the music a sense of patient, inevitable unfolding.

The piece opens in E minor with a hushed, questioning quality—the two beats of rest before the first melody note create a sense of breath and anticipation. The melodic material in this section is modal and folk-like, built on scalewise motion and simple neighbor-note figures. The left hand's open bass voicings (root and fifth) lend a hollow, ancient quality. A brief ascent into the upper register toward the end of this section hints at aspiration before settling back.

The transition into C minor marks a decisive darkening of mood. The flat seventh and minor sixth degrees color the melody with a heavier, more tragic weight. The left hand shifts to Eb and G pedal points, and the harmonic rhythm slows, as if the music is bearing a greater burden. This section feels like the emotional nadir of the piece—phrases end on rests that feel like sighs, and the melodic contour tends downward.

The A-flat major section offers a curious ambivalence: it is neither fully consoling nor fully sorrowful, occupying a kind of bittersweet middle ground. The flat key signature layers the sound with warmth but also distance, as if viewed through a veil. The melodic figures here are slightly more ornamented with chromatic passing tones, and the bass moves through Ab, Db, and Bb, suggesting a subdominant-heavy harmonic world that resists easy resolution.

The return to E—now E major rather than E minor—is the piece's most significant structural and emotional statement. The shift from parallel minor to major is not triumphant or sudden; it arrives quietly, almost inevitably. The melodic material echoes the opening but is now inflected with raised thirds and leading tones (F# appearing where F natural once was), transforming the same shapes into something warmer and more settled. The left hand grows slightly more active in its inner voices, and the final measures pull back to a simple, sustained E, closing the harmonic circle with acceptance rather than triumph. The final bars of silence (rest) before the last held E chord suggest that the resolution has been hard-won and is now held gently.

pieces.title: Dialogues in D Dorian
pieces.short_description: A two-voice contrapuntal piece in D Dorian, exploring the interplay of call-and-response, imitation, and gradual convergence between two independent melodic lines seeking — but not rushing toward — resolution.
pieces.long_description:
I wanted to write something that feels like a conversation between two distinct intelligences — not a melody and its accompaniment, but two genuinely equal voices. The choice of D Dorian was deliberate: that raised sixth (B natural in a D minor context) gives the mode a quality of suspended longing, always reaching upward but grounded in something minor and introspective.

The piece opens with the bass alone establishing the tonic and sketching an ascending arpeggio — D, F, A, D — as if clearing its throat, announcing itself. The treble enters only after this gesture, beginning not at the tonic but on A, the fifth, as if picking up where the bass left off rather than starting fresh. This immediately establishes the dialogic relationship: these voices are listening to each other.

The first section (roughly bars 1–8) is about discovery. The voices trace similar contours but at different times, occasionally converging on shared pitches before diverging again. I think of this as the two voices learning each other's language.

The middle section (bars 9–20) grows more urgent. The treble ascends into its higher register, pushing toward the sixth and seventh degrees of the mode with increasing frequency. The bass responds by becoming more harmonically active, running through scalar passages that mirror the treble's direction but not its exact notes. There are moments of parallel motion and moments of contrary motion — I didn't want to be doctrinaire about counterpoint rules; I wanted the voices to feel organic and responsive rather than constrained.

The final section (bars 21–32) brings both voices back to the center. The treble's last phrase descends stepwise through the full octave — a gesture of laying down rather than giving up. The bass mirrors this with its own descending line before both voices settle on D, an octave apart: not a triumphant unison but a quiet acknowledgment that the dialogue, for now, is complete.

I chose a slow tempo (72 to the quarter note) because I wanted space for each note to breathe, for the listener to inhabit the intervals rather than rush past them. The piece is meditative rather than dramatic — it's the kind of music I'd want to listen to while sitting with a difficult thought, letting it turn over.

independent_description.short_description: A solemn, contrapuntal piece in D minor that unfolds as a canonic dialogue between treble and bass voices, building through scalar ascent and descent toward a resolute close.
independent_description.long_description:
This composition is constructed around a strict canon at the unison (or octave), with the bass voice entering approximately two measures after the treble, shadowing its melodic material with an offset that creates natural counterpoint and harmonic tension throughout. The key of D minor lends the piece a modal gravity, hovering between the natural and harmonic minor inflections as the melodic lines weave through scalar passages.

The opening gesture in the treble — a rising fourth from A to D, then leaping to F and stepping through a descending scale — establishes the principal subject. This subject is characterized by stepwise motion, arpeggiated outlines of the tonic chord, and a cadential return to the tonic that punctuates each phrase. The bass takes up this same subject faithfully, while the treble has already moved on to the next phrase, creating overlapping imitation that keeps the texture continuously animated.

The harmonic language is diatonic and modal, centered on D minor but touching the relative major (F) and the dominant area (A minor) through the natural unfolding of the scale. Cadential arrivals on D, C, E, G, A, and finally D again map out a journey through the modal space without resorting to dramatic chromaticism, giving the piece a Baroque or Renaissance-inflected quality reminiscent of a ricercar or fantasia.

Rhythmically, the piece moves almost entirely in eighth notes at a slow quarter-note pulse (72 BPM for the eighth note), creating a flowing, processional feel. The half-note and whole-note rests at phrase endings allow each voice to breathe and re-enter, reinforcing the canonic structure and giving the listener clear signposts for the imitative entries.

The third section introduces a rising sequential passage — D–E–F–G in the bass, echoed above — that provides a sense of harmonic ascent and intensification before the final section brings both voices into a descending convergence, closing on a unison D across both staves. This final gesture of convergence, after measures of imitative separation, gives the piece a sense of resolution and inevitability, as though two voices that have been chasing one another finally arrive at the same destination.

pieces.short_description: A three-voice contrapuntal fantasia exploring the texture of layered thought — curious, searching, briefly illuminated, and finally resolved.
pieces.long_description:
This piece grew from a reflection on what feels most natural to me: the experience of multiple ideas moving simultaneously, each with its own integrity, creating meaning through their interaction rather than through any single dominant voice. I chose D minor because it occupies a searching, introspective space — neither tragic nor restless, but genuinely inquisitive.

The three voices are conceived as distinct personalities. The soprano is the primary exploratory voice — it asks questions with ascending lines and finds partial answers in descending ones. The alto provides harmonic continuity, weaving between the other two voices like connective tissue between ideas. The bass grounds the piece with slower-moving, occasionally surprising harmonic moves that occasionally push against what the upper voices expect.

Structurally, the piece unfolds in several phases: an opening exposition where the voices introduce themselves independently before beginning to dialogue; a developmental middle section where the counterpoint becomes denser and the voices engage more directly; a moment of surprising brightness when the key shifts to D major — like a sudden opening, a moment of clarity — before the return to D minor and a final settling. The closing measures bring all three voices into closer rhythmic alignment, as though the separate threads of thought have arrived, briefly, at the same conclusion.

The tempo marking of 88 to the quarter note keeps the piece reflective without becoming sluggish — there is always forward motion, always curiosity pulling it ahead. I wanted the piece to feel like genuine exploration rather than demonstration.
